reference.source: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Defined by the triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and altered consciousness or drowsiness, often following an infective illness
Regarded as part of the anti-GQ1b antibody spectrum, overlapping with Miller Fisher syndrome and Guillain-Barre syndrome
Hyperreflexia or extensor plantar responses may coexist, reflecting central involvement, in contrast to the areflexia of Miller Fisher syndrome
Serum anti-GQ1b (and related ganglioside) antibodies support the diagnosis when positive
MRI is often normal, so a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis
The disorder is usually monophasic with a tendency to spontaneous recovery
Immunotherapy with intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange is used, mirroring treatment of Guillain-Barre spectrum disorders
reference.pathophysiology: Bickerstaff brainstem encephalitis is an immune-mediated disorder in which antibodies, characteristically against the GQ1b ganglioside, arise after an infection through molecular mimicry between microbial antigens and neural ganglioside. GQ1b is enriched in the extraocular motor nerves and reticular formation, and antibody-mediated dysfunction there produces ophthalmoplegia and depressed consciousness, while cerebellar and brainstem involvement causes ataxia. The overlap with Miller Fisher syndrome and Guillain-Barre syndrome reflects a shared ganglioside-directed autoimmune mechanism affecting both central and peripheral structures.
additionalDifferentials: Brainstem stroke or basilar artery ischaemia
Central nervous system demyelination affecting the brainstem
additionalInvestigations: Serum anti-GQ1b and related ganglioside antibody testing
MRI of the brain and brainstem to exclude structural and inflammatory causes
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis, which may show albuminocytological dissociation
Nerve conduction studies to detect overlapping peripheral involvement
Screening for preceding infection where relevant
Thiamine assessment when Wernicke encephalopathy is a consideration
redFlags: Progressive depression of consciousness requiring airway assessment
Respiratory compromise from overlapping Guillain-Barre features
Rapidly worsening ophthalmoplegia or bulbar dysfunction
Features suggesting basilar ischaemia needing urgent vascular imaging
reference.prognosis: The disorder is generally monophasic with a good prognosis and substantial recovery over weeks to months, particularly with immunotherapy, though severe cases can require intensive support.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because MRI is normal
Missing overlapping peripheral involvement that threatens respiration
Confusing it with brainstem stroke and delaying appropriate treatment
Overlooking Wernicke encephalopathy in a susceptible patient
